picks.style: ancient greek tragedy, lyre and aulos, low frame drum, single grave male voice, measured, incantatory, slow build
picks.why: Prometheus' unbroken account of men who had eyes but saw nothing and dwelt like ants in sunless caves — a tagless monologue with real images.

picks.style: ancient greek tragic finale, aulos, thunderous frame drums, defiant baritone over layered chorus, slow then storming
picks.why: The closing defiance — let the lightning come, let the sea mingle with the stars — the most quoted moment in the play.

picks.style: roman stage prologue, tibia pipes, plucked lyre, declamatory male voice with a wry lilt, stately, moderate
picks.why: Arcturus the star introduces himself and Jove's ledger of perjurers — a self-contained speech with a genuinely strange conceit.

picks.style: latin didactic verse set to music, lyre and low winds, swelling strings, grave male voice, slow, ominous
picks.why: The weather-omens: heaving sea, herons fleeing the abyss, the nightingale pouring predictions of evil — pure image, no argument.

picks.style: prophetic lament, aulos and frame drum, wild high female voice, accelerating, ecstatic dread
picks.why: Cassandra's raving — 'It comes! it comes! that bloody torch' — urgent, repetitive, made to be sung.

picks.style: roman satiric song, plucked lyre and hand drum, sardonic baritone, brisk, mock-solemn opening
picks.why: Opens on the power that creates all things and takes all back, then turns to the fig Cicero doesn't give for astrologers and dream-sellers.

picks.style: georgian parlour ballad, fortepiano and harp, clear soprano, minor key, unhurried
picks.why: The close of the Two Lovers tale — lilies cropt by an untimely storm, one common tomb, the chapel that still bears their name.

picks.style: melancholy english art song, harpsichord and viol da gamba, plaintive soprano, slow, elegiac
picks.why: Invocation of Death as the certain cure and kind soother — clean quatrains with a refrain-like address.

picks.style: ancient greek lament, kithara and soft drone, low female voice, rocking lullaby pulse, hushed, sorrowful
picks.why: Danaë adrift in the chest with the sleeping Perseus — 'let the sea sleep, let the measureless evil sleep'.

picks.style: ancient greek lyric, barbitos lyre, single female voice, intimate, invocatory, slow
picks.why: Sappho's Aphrodite answering with a smile — 'if she flees, soon she shall pursue' — the most famous lyric in the treatise.

picks.style: greek elegiac declamation, aulos and lyre, stern male chorus, marching cadence, gathering force
picks.why: Carries Solon's elegy whole — not by Zeus but by her own citizens shall Athens fall — rhymed, driving, quotable.

picks.style: late antique latin plainchant, sparse organum drone, solo male voice, austere, very slow
picks.why: Only candidate; the Virgilian tags it strings together ('Let each man be drawn by his own pleasure') still carry a chantable line.

picks.style: victorian art song, piano and cello, subdued baritone, slow, desolate
picks.why: The Coleridge lines Mill reached for in his breakdown — grief without a pang, work without hope drawing nectar in a sieve.
